title: SYSK Selects: How Schizophrenia Works
summary: A SYSK Selects rerun of the episode on schizophrenia. Josh introduces it, then the hosts cover the history of the diagnosis (Kraepelin's dementia praecox classification, Bleuler's 1911 coinage from Greek words for split and mind), how it differs from dissociative identity disorder (split personality), onset age, positive and negative symptoms, avolition, DSM subtypes (paranoid, disorganized/hebephrenic, catatonic, undifferentiated, residual, schizoaffective), delusions versus hallucinations including auditory voices and command hallucinations, suicide and violence risk, outcome statistics, advice for talking with schizophrenic people and their families, cross-cultural recovery rates from WHO studies, famous people (Sid Barrett, John Nash, Jack Kerouac, Wesley Willis, Lionel Aldridge), causes (genetics, prenatal infection, birth month effect, toxoplasmosis theory), brain research, antipsychotic history and side effects, ECT, early intervention in the prodrome, and a listener corrections segment.

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Selects episode, notes outdated terminology, and gives a Wesley Willis clip. The hosts banter about Bob Dylan and David Bowie, then Josh explains his news-based intro: schizophrenia is misunderstood, heavily prescribed, and underfunded.

segments.title: Outcomes, onset, and history of the diagnosis
segments.summary: The hosts discuss homelessness, incarceration, and nursing home statistics for people with schizophrenia. They cover the history: Kraepelin classified it as a dementia, and Bleuler coined the name from Greek words for split and mind. The hosts distinguish it from split personality (dissociative identity disorder). Onset typically comes in late teens to early twenties for men and mid-twenties to early thirties for women, with about a one percent general population risk.

segments.title: Positive and negative symptoms and subtypes
segments.summary: The hosts explain positive symptoms (exaggerated behavior) and negative symptoms (absence of normal behavior), including cognitive symptoms and avolition. They describe the six-month DSM duration requirement and the schizophreniform shorter form. They then list subtypes: paranoid, disorganized (hebephrenic), catatonic, undifferentiated, residual, and schizoaffective disorder.

segments.title: Delusions, hallucinations, and command voices
segments.summary: The hosts define delusions as false beliefs and hallucinations as false sensations. Auditory hallucinations, especially voices, are the most common, and can be single words, mumbling, commentary, or arguing voices. Command hallucinations can be innocuous or dangerous, and most people with dangerous commands are able to resist them. Touch hallucinations and delusions of reference are also described.

segments.title: Outcomes, suicide, violence, and talking with people with schizophrenia
segments.summary: The hosts cite outcome data: after ten years, a majority are recovered or much improved, about ten percent are unimproved, and about ten percent die, mostly by suicide, which is far above the general population rate. They discuss that violence is mostly self-directed or within the home, and that the risk is tied to prior violence and drug or alcohol use. NIMH guidance suggests respectfully disagreeing with delusions rather than contesting or agreeing with them.

segments.title: Recovery in the developing world and famous people with schizophrenia
segments.summary: The hosts describe a WHO study finding higher recovery rates in developing nations, possibly due to less stigma and more accepting work settings. They then discuss famous figures: Sid Barrett of Pink Floyd, John Nash of A Beautiful Mind, Jack Kerouac (disputed diagnosis), Pop Benny's death from drinking, Wesley Willis, and Lionel Aldridge.

segments.title: Causes: genetics, prenatal infection, and brain research
segments.summary: The hosts discuss genetic factors (DISC1, dysbindin, neuregulin, G72 genes) and environmental factors, including the birth month effect, the flu and toxoplasmosis in-utero theory, inflamed white blood cells in brains, and a retrovirus hypothesis. They also cover a New South Wales study on the ventral striatum and reward-based decision making.

segments.title: Treatment: antipsychotics, ECT, family support, and early intervention
segments.summary: The hosts trace antipsychotic history from dopamine focus to glutamate after PCP research, and note side effects like weight gain, drowsiness, and muscle spasms. They mention that about 100,000 Americans a year receive ECT, the role of family support and small goals, and early treatment during the prodrome, including a British doctor's program in two towns that lowered prevalence.

segments.title: Closing resources and population statistic
segments.summary: The hosts close the main discussion with a statistic that a city of three million has over 21,000 people with schizophrenia, suggest compassion, and recommend the schizophrenia.com site, the Daddy of Rock and Roll documentary, and the Harper's article by Rachel Lyon Lviv.

segments.title: Listener corrections segment
segments.summary: The hosts read corrections: the flashpoint of paper is Fahrenheit 451 (not 451 is F), the first murderer note about Billington and an earlier European execution, a Georgia wildfire clarification, a Hinduism correction about one universal Brahman and karma, and a Jainism pronunciation debate.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck wrap up, inviting listeners to send corrections via Facebook, Twitter, or email, and point to HowStuffWorks for more.
